item.title: New Property Investor, Known Name: Building Credibility From Day One
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Entering the UK property investment market for the first time involves navigating complex financial decisions, legal considerations and operational challenges. Whilst these practical elements take priority, many new investors overlook the importance of establishing professional credibility early in their journey. A well-presented personal brand can facilitate smoother interactions with estate agents, mortgage brokers and tradespeople - relationships that often prove crucial for long-term success.

Why First Impressions Matter in Property Investment

Unlike traditional homeowners, property investors frequently engage with multiple professionals who assess their reliability and commitment. Estate agents may prioritise serious investors when lucrative opportunities arise, whilst contractors often quote more competitively for clients who present themselves professionally. Even before building a substantial portfolio, new investors might consider how their communication style and branding could influence these key relationships.

Several straightforward steps could help establish credibility:

  • Creating professional contact details separate from personal accounts
  • Developing consistent branding across emails and documentation
  • Investing in quality business cards for in-person meetings
  • Maintaining a professional online presence on relevant platforms

Building Trust During the Early Stages

For those just starting their investment journey, demonstrating commitment can sometimes outweigh actual portfolio size. Mortgage brokers and lenders often view professionalism as an indicator of responsible borrowing, which could potentially influence product offers or lending decisions. Similarly, experienced investors considering joint ventures typically assess personal reliability before financial capacity.

Property professionals frequently note that the most successful investors combine financial acumen with strong relationship-building skills. Whilst property performance ultimately depends on market factors and financial strategy, the human element of deal-making should not be underestimated - particularly during those crucial early transactions that shape an investor's reputation.

As with any business venture, first impressions in property investment can have lasting consequences. By establishing professional credibility from the outset, new investors may find they secure better opportunities and build more productive working relationships as their portfolios grow.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK property market is seeing notable shifts as experienced professionals take on new roles, bringing fresh expertise to the Midlands and Derbyshire regions. These appointments reflect a growing emphasis on personalised service and strategic expansion within the sector.

Chartwell Noble Welcomes Industry Veteran

Chartwell Noble has announced the appointment of Christian Sanders as a partner agent, marking a significant addition to its team. With over 35 years of experience in residential and rural property, Sanders brings a wealth of knowledge to the role. His career spans agency leadership, business ownership, and advisory positions, including a tenure at Fisher German’s Rural and Residential Agency Department. There, he specialised in the sale of country houses, farms, and estates.

Prior to joining Chartwell Noble, Sanders ran his own agency, John Sanders, which focused on country house sales and property auctions across the Midlands. His decision to align with Chartwell Noble stems from the firm’s emphasis on independence, premium marketing, and client-centric values. Sanders commented, “Chartwell Noble offers the perfect balance of independence and support, allowing me to deliver exceptional results for clients.”

This appointment coincides with Chartwell Noble’s ongoing expansion of its partner agent model, which aims to provide a more personalised and relationship-driven approach to property transactions.

Knight Frank Strengthens Derbyshire Presence

In another key development, Knight Frank has appointed Victoria McLaughlin as its new sales director for Derbyshire. McLaughlin brings 15 years of experience in the property sector, with a focus on higher-value and distinctive homes. Based in Melbourne, Derbyshire, she will spearhead the agency’s efforts to grow its market share and build strong relationships with buyers and sellers across the region.

McLaughlin expressed enthusiasm for her new role, stating, “Melbourne provides an excellent base to serve clients, and I look forward to establishing Knight Frank’s presence in this important market.” Her appointment underscores the firm’s commitment to expanding its footprint in Derbyshire.

Mitchell Glassey, Knight Frank’s director for the West Midlands, highlighted McLaughlin’s local market knowledge and expertise as key assets in achieving the firm’s growth objectives. “Victoria’s experience will be instrumental in driving our business forward in Derbyshire,” he said.

These appointments highlight the evolving dynamics of the UK property market, where experienced professionals are stepping into roles that prioritise client relationships and strategic growth. Homeowners and investors in the Midlands and Derbyshire regions may benefit from the enhanced expertise and tailored services these industry veterans bring to their respective firms.

item.title: One in three rentals include bills in this region – but where is it?
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

New research reveals significant regional variations in whether rental properties are marketed with bills included. According to analysis by LegalforLandlords, the North East leads the way, with over a third (34.4%) of rental listings including bills. This contrasts sharply with Scotland, where just 8.6% of properties offer this arrangement. Across Britain, only 14.9% of rental listings bundle bills with rent, meaning the vast majority of tenants remain responsible for organising and paying utilities separately.

Regional Differences in Bills-Included Rentals

The findings highlight a clear regional divide in how landlords structure tenancies. Whilst the North East dominates with more than one in three properties including bills, Scotland lags behind with fewer than one in ten. London accounts for 23.9% of all bills-included properties nationwide, and the South East represents 13.2%. However, these figures reflect each region’s share of the total bills-included stock rather than the proportion of local listings offering this arrangement.

This disparity suggests that bills-included renting remains concentrated in specific markets rather than becoming a widespread practice across the private rented sector. Certain segments, such as student accommodation and build-to-rent developments, have already embraced this model. For students, the simplicity of a single payment can be a significant draw, whilst build-to-rent operators often use it as a selling point to attract tenants.

Pros and Cons for Tenants and Landlords

For renters, bills-included arrangements can simplify budgeting by providing a fixed monthly payment that covers both rent and utilities. This eliminates the need to manage separate bills for energy, water, and other household expenses. However, landlords who adopt this model take on the responsibility of fluctuating utility costs, which can be influenced by factors such as tenant usage and energy price changes.

The research comes at a time when energy prices are set to rise once again. From October, the energy price cap will increase by 4%, taking the annual cost for a typical household paying by Direct Debit from £1,663 to £1,723. This adds another layer of complexity for landlords considering whether to include bills in their rental agreements.

Sim Sekhon, group CEO of LegalforLandlords, commented: “Bills-included renting clearly isn’t a single national trend. In the North East, it accounts for more than a third of rental listings, while in Scotland it is less than one in ten. That’s a substantial difference in how landlords are approaching the rental proposition.”

Ultimately, the decision to include bills within rent depends on various factors, including regional market conditions, tenant preferences, and landlords’ willingness to absorb utility costs. Homeowners may wish to consider these dynamics when deciding how to structure their rental agreements.

item.title: The Masterplan: Oasis star Noel Gallagher gets green light for property overhaul
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Oasis musician Noel Gallagher has received planning permission to restore and modernise his £11.5 million Grade II-listed London mansion, whilst balancing conservation with contemporary comforts. Westminster City Council approved extensive renovations for the mid-19th century property, which has suffered from structural issues including damp and a deteriorating roof over its long history.

A Heritage Property Transformation

The seven-bedroom Hampstead home, spanning five storeys, has seen multiple alterations over the decades – from conversion into flats before being restored as a single residence, to what planning documents describe as "unsympathetic" modifications. Gallagher's approved scheme focuses on repairing the historic fabric while introducing thoughtful upgrades. Architects will preserve original period features such as panelling, cornices and architraves, alongside essential structural repairs.

Modern additions include a basement entertainment space with a bar, cinema room, gym and sauna – plus a one-bedroom guest suite created from an adjoining building. The rear extension will also undergo redesigns. Planning officers highlighted that the sensitive approach would cause no harm to the property's architectural significance, even noting potential "modest enhancement" through improved window details.

Sustainable Meets Traditional

Beyond luxury amenities, the renovation incorporates several eco-conscious measures. Slimline double glazing, enhanced roof insulation and upgraded building services aim to improve energy efficiency. Westminster Council stipulated that all exterior work must precisely match the original building's materials and craftsmanship – a condition Gallagher's team will meet whilst prioritising reuse of demolition materials where possible.

This ambitious project coincides with Oasis's reunion tour announcements, ensuring Gallagher juggles property renovations with a hectic performance schedule. Contractors have already begun preparatory interior strip-outs ahead of the conservation-led refurbishment.

The musician's property venture follows his brother Liam's purchase of an eight-bedroom Cotswolds estate earlier this year. For listed building owners considering renovations, Gallagher's approved plans demonstrate how heritage preservation and modern living can harmoniously coexist with careful planning.

item.title: Could upfront surveys in sales packs finally speed up property transactions?
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New proposals to introduce upfront property surveys could significantly streamline the homebuying process in England and Wales. Landmark Information Group has launched Sales Pack Ready Surveys, a service allowing estate agents and property professionals to access property condition reports before transactions progress.

Addressing delays in property transactions

Recent data from TwentyCi highlights that nearly a quarter of agreed property sales fail to complete, often due to issues emerging late in the process. These unexpected problems can lead to extended negotiations, delayed exchanges or even collapsed sales. The new initiative aims to tackle these challenges by:

  • Providing RICS-standard condition reports at the start of the sales process
  • Identifying visible defects and maintenance concerns earlier
  • Reducing the likelihood of last-minute price renegotiations

Nick Dyoss of Landmark Information Group commented: "The property industry can't afford to wait for reforms to take effect before improving how transactions work. Businesses adapting now will be better positioned as changes become embedded in the homebuying process."

Shifting towards informed decision-making

The initiative aligns with the government's broader push to make more property information available upfront. Under these proposals, survey reports would form part of a comprehensive sales pack alongside title details, legal documents and local searches.

This approach could help both buyers and sellers make more informed decisions before committing significant time and money to a transaction. As Dyoss noted: "The future involves helping parties uncover potential issues before a sale progresses, rather than discovering problems mid-transaction."

Industry experts suggest this move towards transparency might:

  • Reduce the average time between offer and completion
  • Minimise the number of failed transactions
  • Create a more efficient property market overall

Industry-wide adoption on the horizon

The surveying profession is actively exploring how upfront condition reports could become standard practice. Later this month, Project 28 Charter members will host a roundtable discussion examining how to deliver property condition information at scale.

Landmark's national partnership model aims to make these surveys widely accessible, potentially transforming how properties are marketed and purchased. As the market evolves, early adopters of this approach may gain a competitive advantage in an increasingly transparent property landscape.

While these developments won't eliminate all transaction delays, they represent a significant step towards reducing unnecessary hold-ups in the homebuying process. Homeowners considering a sale might wish to discuss upfront survey options with their estate agent as the market continues to modernise.

item.title: Housing market warning as sales fall for fourth consecutive month
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The UK housing market continues to show signs of cooling, with new data revealing a fourth consecutive monthly decline in agreed sales during August. While completed transactions currently appear resilient, analysts warn this reflects earlier market activity rather than current conditions.

Sales pipeline weakens as listings surge

TwentyCi's latest figures indicate agreed sales in August were 6% lower than the same period last year, following year-on-year drops of 8% in May and June, then 5% in July. Cumulatively, the first eight months of 2026 have seen 5.4% fewer agreed sales compared to 2025.

Meanwhile, property listings have reached their highest level in a decade, rising 2.1% year-on-year. This combination of fewer buyers and more available properties is creating increased competition among sellers whilst improving choice for prospective purchasers.

Colin Bradshaw, TwentyCi CEO, notes: "Surface-level transaction figures suggest resilience, but our sales agreed data tells a different story. We've seen consistent year-on-year demand reductions exceeding 5% since May - this sustained weakness will impact future completions."

Market balance shifts towards buyers

The widening gap between supply and demand appears to be tilting negotiating power towards buyers. TwentyCi reports deteriorating demand-to-supply ratios across all major property types, with flats experiencing the most pronounced shift at 13.2% lower demand year-on-year.

Separate Sprift data showing improved sales conversion rates requires context - this reflects new listings falling faster than sales agreed during August rather than increased market activity. The national picture suggests buyers are becoming more selective, taking longer to commit amidst greater choice.

HMRC's more positive transaction figures for July (5% higher year-on-year) largely represent deals negotiated during stronger market conditions earlier in 2026. TwentyCi forecasts 1.16 million residential transactions for the full year - 3.9% below 2025's total but still 5.6% above 2024 levels.

Affordability pressures persist

With Bank of England base rate decisions continuing to influence mortgage costs, affordability constraints remain a key factor dampening market activity. Homeowners considering a move may wish to monitor how these shifting market dynamics affect both selling prospects and purchasing power.

Those planning transactions might find it valuable to research local market conditions thoroughly, as regional variations mean some areas could buck the national trend. Mortgage borrowers could also benefit from reviewing their options, with some lenders potentially becoming more competitive as seller competition intensifies.

As we approach autumn - traditionally a busier period for the property market - all eyes will be on whether these emerging trends consolidate or whether seasonal factors help rebalance activity levels.

item.title: Property sales conversion hits six-month high as new listings plunge
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The UK property market has shown signs of resilience, with the sales conversion rate reaching its highest level in six months, according to Sprift’s latest Sales Market Intelligence Report. Whilst new listings across Great Britain fell by 11.6% in August, the number of sales agreed dropped by a smaller 7.2%, pushing the national conversion rate up to 57.3%. This marks the highest figure since February, indicating a shift in market dynamics.

Regional Variations in Conversion Rates

Despite the overall improvement, significant regional disparities persist. Scotland led the way with a conversion rate of 74.8%, closely followed by the North East at 64.3% and Wales at 62.7%. In stark contrast, London lagged behind with just 40.8% of new listings converting to sales – 34 percentage points lower than Scotland. Eight out of 11 regions recorded conversion rates above the national average, highlighting the challenges faced by vendors and agents in London.

London also has the largest backlog of unsold properties, with 13,157 listings remaining unconverted in August. This compares to just 2,501 in the North East. Pricing pressures are particularly evident in southern England, with the South East and London recording the highest proportions of reduced listings at 43% and 41.2% respectively. Scotland, meanwhile, had the lowest rate of price reductions at just 22.3%.

Market Trends and Challenges

Across Great Britain, total for-sale stock now stands at 741,504 properties, with homes spending an average of 159 days on the market. However, there are notable differences by property type and location. Semi-detached homes in Scotland averaged just 94 days on the market, whilst flats in the North West took 225 days to sell. These variations underscore the complexity of the current market landscape.

Planning applications also saw a decline in August, falling by 8.8% to 17,947. Despite this, the approval rate edged up to 85.7% of applications determined. Matt Gilpin, founder and CEO of Sprift, noted the contrasting markets within the UK, stating: “August is a reminder that a six-month high for the country as a whole still hides two very different markets underneath it.”

As the market continues to evolve, homeowners may wish to consider regional trends and pricing strategies to maximise their chances of securing a sale. With mortgage rates remaining relatively stable, borrowers might find opportunities to navigate the market more effectively.

item.title: Why 5pm rarely means the end of the working day for agents
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

For letting agents and property managers, the working day rarely ends at 5pm. New data reveals that tenants logged half of all maintenance cases outside traditional office hours during the summer months, highlighting the growing demand for out-of-hours support. Between June and August 2026, 17.4% of reports were submitted at weekends, adding to the workload for those managing rental properties.

Heating and hot-water issues dominate after hours

Heating and hot-water problems were particularly prevalent outside standard working hours, with 73.1% of cases reported during evenings, nights, or weekends. For issues involving a loss of hot water, this figure rose to 73.7%. Urgent maintenance requests also frequently occurred after hours, with 57.5% of High or Emergency cases reported outside Monday-to-Friday, 9am-to-5pm office hours.

Connor Hawkins, chief solutions officer at Lettie, commented on the findings: “Maintenance demands don’t stop at 5pm, but the scale of out-of-hours requests is striking. When almost three-quarters of hot-water disruptions occur outside traditional working hours, this trend can no longer be seen as an exception.”

Plumbing and drainage top the list of summer issues

item.title: Landlords favour familiar territory as investment strategies shift
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

UK landlords are increasingly favouring investments in their local areas, opting for familiar markets over higher-yielding opportunities further afield, according to new research. The trend suggests a strategic shift towards leveraging local expertise amid rising costs and regulatory complexity in the private rental sector.

The appeal of local knowledge

Analysis of landlord investment patterns reveals a notable move towards regional concentration, with the East Midlands and South West seeing particularly strong growth in local property acquisitions. Experts suggest this reflects a growing preference for markets where landlords already have established knowledge of:

  • Local rental values and tenant demand
  • Council licensing requirements, especially for HMOs
  • Reliable tradespeople and letting agents
  • Neighbourhood-specific property trends

This localised approach contrasts with previous strategies that often prioritised chasing the highest yields nationwide. While Wales saw a decline in local investment, most regions experienced increased activity from landlords choosing to expand within their existing areas of operation.

Adapting to market changes

The buy-to-let landscape has undergone significant transformation in recent years, with professional landlords facing:

  • Higher mortgage costs following base rate increases
  • Expanded regulatory requirements
  • Growing tenant expectations around property standards
  • Tax changes affecting profitability calculations

In this more challenging environment, regional specialists may benefit from advantages that national investors lack. Local landlords often have better insight into micro-market conditions, from identifying undervalued properties to anticipating shifts in tenant preferences. Many have also established networks of trusted professionals, potentially reducing management costs and void periods.

Property professionals note that successful landlords are taking a more sophisticated approach to portfolio building, considering factors like:

  • Long-term capital growth potential alongside rental yields
  • Operational efficiencies from geographic concentration
  • Diversification across property types and tenures
  • Exit strategy viability for different asset classes

As the market continues to evolve, local expertise appears to be emerging as a key differentiator for landlords navigating today's more complex buy-to-let environment.

item.title: Average UK rents reach a record high
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New figures reveal that average rental prices across the UK have hit unprecedented levels, with tenants facing increasing pressure on their finances. The sustained rise in housing costs affects most regions, compounding challenges for households already grappling with higher living expenses.

Regional variations in rental growth

Whilst rents are climbing nationwide, the increases vary significantly between locations. Major cities and commuter hubs continue to see the most substantial jumps, particularly in the South East where demand consistently outstrips supply. However, even traditionally more affordable areas are experiencing notable hikes, leaving fewer low-cost options for renters.

Industry analysts highlight several factors contributing to the trend:

  • Strong tenant demand from young professionals and families
  • Limited new rental property construction
  • Some landlords exiting the market due to regulatory changes
  • Higher mortgage costs being passed through to tenants

Potential strategies for renters

With rental costs consuming a growing portion of household income, tenants might consider several approaches to manage expenses. Some explore properties in neighbouring areas where rents may be lower, albeit potentially with longer commute times. Others assess whether house-sharing could provide temporary financial relief.

Prospective renters may wish to:

  • Research local market trends before committing to a new lease
  • Factor in potential future increases when budgeting
  • Review tenancy agreement terms regarding rent review clauses
  • Consider negotiating longer tenancies in exchange for fixed rents

For those able to do so, building a savings buffer could provide flexibility if rents continue rising. Meanwhile, first-time buyers might reassess whether current market conditions make purchasing marginally more accessible than continuing to rent in some regions.

As the rental market evolves, staying informed about local conditions and understanding contractual obligations remain crucial for tenants navigating these challenging conditions.

item.title: RICS August survey suggests market improvements
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The latest Residential Market Survey from the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS) indicates cautious optimism in the UK housing market, with signs of gradual recovery emerging in August. Whilst challenges remain, the report highlights modest improvements in buyer activity alongside ongoing rental market pressures that continue to push prices upwards.

Encouraging signs in sales market

RICS data suggests a tentative uptick in property transactions, with new buyer enquiries showing improvement for the first time in several months. Surveyors reported marginally more positive sentiment amongst potential purchasers, potentially reflecting growing confidence as mortgage rates stabilise below last year's peaks. The national picture remains mixed, however, with some regions demonstrating clearer signs of recovery than others.

Properties are still taking slightly longer to sell compared to the frenetic pandemic market, but the average time on market appears to be stabilising. Pricing indicators also show modest progress, with the net balance for price expectations moving into slightly positive territory after prolonged negative readings. This suggests surveyors anticipate prices may hold steady or see minor increases in coming months rather than significant declines.

Rental market challenges persist

The August survey paints a less encouraging picture for tenants, with rental supply failing to keep pace with demand. A net balance of 58% of contributors reported rising tenant demand, whilst 35% noted a decline in landlord instructions. This imbalance continues to exert upward pressure on rents across most UK regions.

Several factors contribute to the rental sector squeeze, including:

  • Landlords exiting the market due to regulatory changes and tax adjustments
  • Higher mortgage costs reducing buy-to-let profitability
  • Persistent undersupply of new rental properties entering the market

With no immediate solution to this supply-demand mismatch, RICS members anticipate further rental growth in the near term, potentially adding to affordability challenges for many tenants.

As autumn approaches, market watchers will be keen to see whether the tentative improvements in sales activity develop into a more sustained recovery, and whether policymakers can address the structural issues affecting the rental sector. For now, the market appears to be finding its footing after a turbulent period, albeit with significant regional variations.

item.title: Confidence returns to London property market
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
London Property Market Shows Signs of Renewed Optimism

The capital's housing market is demonstrating encouraging signs of recovery as recent reports indicate strengthening activity among buyers, tenants and sellers. After a period of uncertainty, improving sentiment suggests a gradual return of confidence in London's property sector.

Market Activity Gains Momentum

Data from across the capital reveals increased movement in the property market, with notable rises in both rental and sales enquiries. Estate agents report growing numbers of viewings and transactions, suggesting that prospective homeowners and investors are regaining their appetite for London properties. This uptick follows several months of cautious market behaviour during economic uncertainties.

The rental market is seeing particular vitality, with demand from tenants matching the increased availability of rental properties. This balanced dynamic could help stabilise rental prices after recent fluctuations. For those considering buy-to-let investments, the current conditions might present interesting opportunities to enter the market.

What This Means for Potential Buyers and Sellers

For homeowners contemplating selling their London properties, the improved market sentiment could be welcome news. With more buyers actively searching, properties may spend less time on the market, though pricing remains crucial. Those looking to sell might wish to consult local agents for up-to-date valuations reflecting current demand.

Prospective buyers could find the market increasingly competitive as activity picks up. Mortgage applicants may want to ensure their finances are in order, including having agreement in principle arranged where possible. While interest rates remain elevated compared to recent historic lows, some stability in the lending market could make financial planning somewhat easier.

As with any property decision, conducting thorough research and seeking independent financial advice remains essential. The London market's recovery appears to be gaining pace, but conditions can vary significantly between boroughs and property types.

item.title: Visitor levy could impact holiday let investors
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

New powers allowing local authorities to implement a visitor levy on overnight stays could have significant implications for holiday let investors across the UK. The measure, set to take effect in 2026, enables councils to charge tourists a small fee per night, potentially affecting the profitability of short-term rental properties.

How the visitor levy works

The visitor levy scheme grants local councils discretionary powers to introduce an overnight charge for tourists staying in accommodation within their boundaries. Similar to tourist taxes seen in European cities, the levy typically amounts to a few pounds per person per night. Funds raised are intended to support local infrastructure and services benefiting tourism, such as maintaining public spaces or improving transport links.

For holiday let owners, these additional costs may need to be absorbed or passed on to guests. Property investors with portfolios in popular tourist destinations might see the greatest impact, particularly in areas where councils choose to implement higher rates. Locations with existing pressure on local services from tourism are most likely to adopt the scheme early.

Potential effects on holiday let investments

Industry experts highlight several considerations for holiday let investors following this announcement:

  • Occupancy rates could be affected if higher accommodation costs deter some visitors
  • Administrative requirements may increase with additional tax collection responsibilities
  • Property yields might decrease slightly where levies cannot be fully passed to guests
  • Location-specific variations could influence investment decisions between different regions

Whilst the financial impact per property may appear modest, those with multiple holiday lets or operating in high-tax areas may notice more substantial effects on their overall returns. The measure comes alongside other recent changes affecting holiday lets, including alterations to mortgage interest relief and planning permission requirements in some areas.

Adapting to the changing landscape

Investors in the holiday let market may wish to review their business plans in light of this development. Monitoring which local authorities implement the levy and at what rate could help inform future purchasing decisions. Some operators might consider adjusting their pricing strategies or marketing approaches to maintain competitiveness if the tourism tax becomes widespread.

The visitor levy forms part of a broader trend of increasing regulation in the short-term rental sector. As the market evolves, staying informed about local policy changes and their potential financial implications remains crucial for holiday let investors seeking to maximise their returns.

With the scheme not coming into force until 2026, investors have time to assess how different councils might implement the charges and factor this into their long-term strategies. Professional financial advice could help those concerned about the potential impact on their portfolios.

item.title: Tribunal cases rise 56% YOY in Q2
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The number of residential property tribunal cases in England and Wales rose by 56% year-on-year during the second quarter of 2024, according to recent government data. This significant increase coincides with the implementation of new tenancy regulations that are transforming the private rental sector.

What's driving the tribunal case surge?

Industry analysts attribute the sharp rise in tribunal activity to several factors. The introduction of the Renters (Reform) Bill provisions has created uncertainty for both landlords and tenants regarding their revised rights and responsibilities. Many cases appear to stem from disputes over property conditions, deposit disagreements, and the interpretation of new eviction procedures.

The Ministry of Justice reported that the most common types of cases involved:

  • Challenges to improvement notices served by local councils
  • Disputes over tenancy deposit protection schemes
  • Appeals against housing benefit decisions
  • Controversies surrounding the new 'no fault' eviction restrictions

Impact on the rental market

Property professionals suggest the tribunal backlog could have wider implications for the housing market. Some landlords may become more cautious about entering or remaining in the private rental sector, potentially reducing available accommodation. Tenants, meanwhile, might face longer waiting times for dispute resolutions as the system adjusts to higher caseloads.

The government has acknowledged the strain on tribunal resources and is considering measures to streamline processes. These could include expanding the digital submission system and increasing the number of qualified adjudicators to handle the growing workload.

For homeowners and landlords navigating these changes, it may be worth familiarising themselves with the updated regulations and seeking professional advice when dealing with tenancy disputes. Mortgage borrowers with buy-to-let properties should particularly stay informed about how these legal developments might affect their obligations and rights as landlords.

As the sector continues to adapt to the legislative changes, both tenants and property investors will need to monitor how these tribunal trends develop in coming quarters.

item.title: Interest rate stability could be coming to an end as markets price in hikes
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The Bank of England is anticipated to maintain the base rate at 3.75% this week, marking the sixth consecutive meeting without a change. However, financial markets are increasingly suggesting that this period of stability may soon end, with predictions of multiple rate hikes over the coming months. Borrowers and homeowners may wish to prepare for potential shifts in mortgage costs as these changes could influence affordability.

Market Predictions Point to Rate Increases

Financial markets are currently pricing in up to four quarter-point increases by July 2024, which could push the base rate to 4.75%. This shift in expectations follows stronger-than-anticipated economic growth and renewed concerns about inflation. Recent data revealed that the UK economy grew by 0.4% in July, surpassing forecasts of stagnation. This resilience suggests the economy may be better equipped to handle higher borrowing costs, but it also increases the likelihood of rate rises to curb inflationary pressures.

Inflation, as measured by the Consumer Prices Index (CPI), rose to 2.9% in July, up from 2.6% in June. This marks the highest level since March and has heightened concerns about the cost of living. Further inflationary pressure is expected when Ofgem’s new energy price cap takes effect in October, with bills set to rise by 4% for typical households. Global energy price increases are also contributing to the uncertainty surrounding the inflation outlook.

Implications for Borrowers and the Housing Market

Should rates rise as predicted, homeowners with variable-rate mortgages could face higher monthly repayments, while prospective buyers may encounter increased borrowing costs. This could impact housing affordability, particularly for first-time buyers or those stretching their budgets. Estate agents and property market participants may need to adapt to a changing environment after months of relative stability in mortgage rates.

The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) is expected to adopt a cautious approach this week, assessing the economic impact of geopolitical tensions and rising energy costs. However, divisions within the committee are already apparent. At the previous meeting, three members—Huw Pill, Megan Greene, and Catherine Mann—voted for an immediate rate increase to 4%. Economists predict these "hawks" may push for another rise this week, though the majority are likely to favour maintaining the current rate.

As the MPC’s decision appears largely settled, attention may instead focus on the committee’s communications and any indications of a shift in stance. Borrowers and homeowners might consider reviewing their financial plans in light of these potential changes, ensuring they are well-prepared for any future adjustments to interest rates.

item.title: Buy-to-let company boom goes into reverse after 18 years
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

The number of new buy-to-let companies in Great Britain is set to decline for the first time in nearly two decades, marking a significant shift in the property investment landscape. According to recent analysis by Hamptons, 41,483 buy-to-let companies were established in the first eight months of 2026, representing an 8% drop compared to the same period in 2025. This trend accelerated in August, with new incorporations falling by 22% year-on-year. If this continues, 2026 will see the first annual decrease in buy-to-let company formations since 2008. Despite this slowdown, the total number of buy-to-let companies continues to rise, reaching 469,165 by the end of August 2026.

What’s Driving the Decline?

The slowdown in new buy-to-let company formations is largely attributed to a reduction in landlords transferring personally owned properties into limited companies. This trend had been fuelled by tax changes introduced in 2016, which limited mortgage interest tax relief for higher-rate taxpayers, making incorporation a more attractive option. However, Hamptons suggests that the market has now reached a peak, with many landlords who stood to benefit from incorporation having already restructured their portfolios.

Transferring properties into a company structure can come with significant upfront costs, including Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT) and Capital Gains Tax. For example, Hamptons estimates that the average SDLT bill for such transfers in 2025 was around £28,000, based on an average property value of £380,000. These costs may be deterring landlords who have yet to make the switch, particularly as the financial advantages of incorporation become less compelling.

item.title: UK rents hit record high as affordability squeeze intensifies
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Rents across the UK have reached record highs, with tenants now dedicating almost a third of their income to housing costs, according to the latest data from HomeLet Rental Index. In August, the average monthly rent climbed to £1,382, marking a 0.9% increase from July’s figure of £1,369. This represents an annual growth of 4.1%, up from £1,328 a year earlier. Excluding Greater London, the average rent stood at £1,179, reflecting a 0.8% monthly rise and a 3.4% annual increase. The trend of rising rents was observed in most regions, with ten out of the twelve markets tracked by HomeLet showing monthly growth.

London Leads as the UK’s Most Expensive Rental Market

Greater London continues to dominate as the most costly rental market in the UK. In August, the average rent in the capital reached £2,238, rising by 1.4% month-on-month and 5.1% year-on-year. Outside London, the South West recorded the strongest annual increase at 5.2%, closely followed by Northern Ireland at 4.9%. Northern Ireland also saw the largest monthly rise at 2.4%, with the South West not far behind at 2.3%. In contrast, Wales was the only region to experience both monthly and annual declines, with average rents dropping by 1% to £925.

Affordability Challenges for Tenants

The rising rents are placing significant financial strain on tenants. HomeLet’s data reveals that renters are now spending an average of 32% of their income on housing costs, with Londoners facing an even higher proportion at 39.8%. Meanwhile, landlords are grappling with their own financial pressures, particularly when tenancies break down. According to Legal for Lettings’ Quarterly CourtWatch for Q2 2026, the average rent loss per possession case stands at £6,411, with court delays averaging 4.85 months across the 63 courts monitored.

Julie Ford CCPM, founder of Lettings Advice Service, noted, “While it is too early to draw definitive conclusions, it is possible that consecutive rent increases reflect the impact of the Renters’ Rights Act on landlord behaviour and market dynamics. With renters already allocating 32% of their income to housing costs, the sector must consider whether continued rent growth is sustainable in an environment where wages are not rising at the same pace and the cost of living continues to squeeze household budgets.”

Iain McKenzie, CEO of The Guild of Property Professionals, added, “The rental market is becoming increasingly complex for landlords, with affordability pressures, changing legislation, and greater expectations around compliance all influencing the decisions they need to make.” As the rental market evolves, both tenants and landlords face challenges that could shape the future of the sector.

item.title: Rental supply falls for first time in three years as rents accelerate
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The UK rental market has seen its first annual decline in available properties for three years, creating tighter conditions that are pushing rents higher across most regions. According to Zoopla's latest Rental Market Report, rental supply has fallen by 3% compared to last year, with August seeing a particularly sharp 6% reduction. At the same time, demand has strengthened to nearly 5.3 enquiries per listing – the highest level since late 2022.

Rental squeeze drives price growth

The imbalance between supply and demand has accelerated rental inflation, with annual growth reaching 2.6% in July – up from 1.6% in February. The average UK rent now stands at £1,340 per month, and analysts forecast this figure could rise by 4-5% annually by 2026. Higher mortgage rates appear to be contributing to the pressure, keeping potential first-time buyers in rental accommodation for longer whilst discouraging landlords from expanding their portfolios.

Regional variations tell an interesting story about market dynamics. Yorkshire and the Humber has experienced a significant 12% drop in rental properties alongside some of the fastest rising rents, while Wales – where supply has increased by 7% – has seen rental growth slow noticeably. These patterns suggest local market fundamentals rather than nationwide policy changes are primarily driving current rental trends.

London faces acute pressures

The capital's rental market shows particularly intense strain, with inner London boroughs seeing available stock fall by 13% alongside rising demand. Annual rental growth in London has accelerated to 2.9%, compared to 1.7% last year. Zoopla's analysis highlights how higher mortgage rates disproportionately affect London's housing market, where buyers now need an extra £35,500 deposit to compensate for increased borrowing costs – significantly above the £18,200 national average.

This perfect storm of factors – constrained supply, robust demand and mortgage market challenges – looks set to maintain upward pressure on rents in the coming months. Homeowners considering becoming landlords might review these market conditions carefully, whilst renters may wish to explore their options sooner rather than later as competition for properties intensifies.

item.title: Landlord Law Newsround #453
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent weeks have seen significant developments affecting landlords and property investors across England and Wales. From new registration schemes to ongoing court delays, those in the private rental sector may wish to take note of several important changes that could impact their lettings businesses.

Mandatory Landlord Registration Scheme Announced

The government has confirmed details of its forthcoming national landlord database, with the rollout beginning in the West Midlands on 15th December this year. The scheme will expand regionally, with each area having a three-month window for landlords to complete their registrations. Key points include:

  • Registration costs £66 per property, renewable annually
  • Only currently let properties require immediate registration
  • Vacant properties must be registered before marketing begins
  • Fines will apply for non-compliance

Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook described the initiative as an important step towards creating a comprehensive private rental sector database that could benefit both tenants and responsible landlords. Property owners may wish to check the official rollout schedule to ensure they meet their local deadline.

Court Delays Reach 20-Year High

Concerns continue to grow over worsening delays in the possession claims process. Recent Ministry of Justice figures reveal the average repossession case now takes up to 27 weeks - the longest waiting period in two decades. Anecdotal evidence suggests some landlords face additional administrative challenges, with one case seeing court documents arrive weeks after the intended possession date.

While overall possession claims have decreased slightly year-on-year, the extended processing times could present cash flow challenges for some landlords. The government has announced plans to transfer rent challenge cases to HMRC's Valuation Office, potentially easing pressure on tribunal services.

Short-Term Let Registration Coming in 2025

From March 2025, operators of short-term holiday lets in England will need to register their properties on a new national database. The scheme will require landlords to provide property details and pay a registration fee, though full pricing details remain forthcoming. Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Secretary Lisa Nandy stated the register aims to help local authorities balance tourism needs with housing availability while strengthening enforcement capabilities.

With multiple new regulatory requirements coming into force, landlords and property investors might consider reviewing their compliance strategies and diaries to prepare for these changes. Staying informed about implementation timelines could help avoid potential penalties and ensure smooth transitions to the new systems.

item.title: Letting agents accused of cashing in with new landlord charges
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Following the implementation of the Renters' Rights Act, some letting agents have reportedly introduced new charges for landlords to cover additional administrative work. Industry bodies warn that these unexpected fees could strain relationships between agents and property investors, whilst others suggest the costs reflect legitimate compliance burdens.

New Fees Emerge Amid Regulatory Changes

The Telegraph has reported cases of letting agents charging separately for services that were previously bundled within standard fees. These include compliance audits, financial statements and paperwork relating to rent increases. The changes come as agents adapt to increased regulatory requirements under the new legislation, which has also reduced traditional income streams like tenancy renewal commissions.

Examples cited include KFH's introduction of a £12+VAT charge for additional financial statements, whilst some agents reportedly levy up to £300 for compliance audits. The British Landlords Association has cautioned landlords to review their agency agreements carefully, noting that whilst increased administration is understandable, "unexpected or questionable add-on fees" may erode trust in the sector.

Mixed Reactions From Industry Voices

Chris Norris of the National Residential Landlords Association suggests some agents may be capitalising on landlords' compliance anxieties: "With significant sanctions for regulatory breaches, many landlords rely heavily on agents to ensure everything is above board – some may see this as an opportunity to introduce additional charges." He acknowledged some landlords might view such practices as "underhand" whilst others accept them as business costs.

Industry data supports these observations, with Goodlord reporting nearly a quarter of landlords have experienced increased agency fees since the reforms. However, letting agents argue the charges reflect genuine additional workloads. Greg Tsuman of Martyn Gerrard lettings commented: "The reforms require more paperwork from both parties. If landlords choose to outsource this compliance work, it's reasonable for agents to charge accordingly."

Navigating the New Fee Landscape

Landlords concerned about changing fee structures might consider:

  • Reviewing agency agreements to understand what services are included
  • Requesting itemised breakdowns of any new charges
  • Comparing service packages across multiple agents
  • Considering whether to handle some compliance tasks directly

As the sector adjusts to the post-reform environment, transparency around fees appears crucial for maintaining positive landlord-agent relationships. Both parties face new administrative challenges, but how these costs are distributed may significantly influence business decisions in the private rental market.
